deep_dives.bottom_line: This large meta-analysis shows that the Phoenix Sepsis Criteria have good prognostic accuracy for in-hospital mortality in children with suspected infection and outperform the IPSCC criteria, but their specificity varies by clinical setting; these findings support the PSC's use for risk stratification rather than early sepsis screening, highlighting the need for further validation in diverse care environments.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: The Phoenix Sepsis Criteria (PSC) show good prognostic accuracy for in-hospital mortality in children with suspected infection and outperform the IPSCC criteria, but performance varies by clinical setting.

- Study type: Systematic review and meta-analysis
- Population/setting: Children under 18 years with suspected infection in hospital settings (15 studies, 16 cohorts, 2,601,038 encounters)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Phoenix Sepsis Criteria (PSC) versus International Pediatric Sepsis Consensus Conference (IPSCC) criteria
- Primary endpoints: Prognostic accuracy for in-hospital mortality
- Key results: PSC pooled sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.67-0.85), specificity 0.73 (95% CI, 0.51-0.87), diagnostic odds ratio 9.2 (95% CI, 5.1-16.8), and AUC 0.81 (95% CI, 0.75-0.84); IPSCC AUC was 0.71 (difference 0.10, 95% CI, 0.04-0.19); PSC specificity was lower in ICU (0.48) than ED (0.99).
- Limitations:
- Performance varies by clinical setting.
- PSC is intended for prognostic risk stratification, not early sepsis screening.
- Further validation needed in ED, ward, and lower-resource settings.
- Why this matters: Accurate prognostic tools like the PSC can improve risk stratification and guide clinical decision-making in pediatric sepsis, but context-specific validation is essential.
deep_dives.title: Prognostic Accuracy of the Phoenix Sepsis Criteria for Mortality in Children With Suspected Infection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This large secondary analysis of the SISPCT randomized trial found that higher plasma H3.1 nucleosome levels at admission independently predict increased risk of 28-day mortality and need for renal replacement therapy in sepsis and septic shock, suggesting H3.1 nucleosomes may serve as clinically useful biomarkers for risk stratification in these patients.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Admission plasma H3.1 nucleosome levels are independently associated with increased risk of 28-day mortality and need for renal replacement therapy in patients with sepsis and septic shock.

- Study type: Secondary analysis of a multicenter randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: 971 patients with sepsis or septic shock from 33 ICUs in Germany (SISPCT trial, 2009-2013)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: No intervention; comparison of plasma H3.1 nucleosome levels at admission
- Primary endpoints: 28-day mortality and requirement for renal replacement therapy (RRT)
- Key results: A one log10 unit increase in H3.1 was associated with a 48% increase in 28-day mortality (adjusted HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.07-2.04, p=0.02) and an 80% increase in risk of 28-day RRT (adjusted HR 1.8, 95% CI 1.34-2.40, p<0.001); H3.1 levels were higher in septic shock vs. sepsis (median 921.84 vs. 432.71 ng/mL, p<0.001) and in those requiring RRT (1832 vs. 801.4 ng/mL, p=0.01).
- Limitations:
- Secondary analysis, not a primary endpoint of the original trial
- Observational associations cannot establish causality
- Potential confounding despite multivariable adjustment
- Why this matters: Identifying biomarkers like H3.1 nucleosomes may help predict which sepsis patients are at higher risk for mortality and need for renal replacement therapy, enabling earlier intervention and risk stratification.
deep_dives.title: H3.1 Nucleosomes to Predict Renal Replacement Therapy and Mortality in Sepsis-A Secondary Analysis of the SISPCT Randomized Control Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This pooled analysis of five large RCTs (n=2563) shows that reductions in IL-6 mediate the mortality benefits of anakinra, imatinib, and low tidal volume ventilation in ARDS and COVID-19, highlighting IL-6 as a key therapeutic target and biomarker for guiding interventions in acute lung injury.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Reduction in plasma IL-6 levels mediates the mortality benefit of anakinra, imatinib, and low tidal volume ventilation in ARDS and COVID-19, highlighting IL-6 as a key therapeutic target.

- Study type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of five randomized controlled trials with joint modeling and meta-analysis.
- Population/setting: 2563 patients with ARDS or COVID-19 from five large randomized controlled trials.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Interventions: imatinib, anakinra, low tidal volume ventilation, high PEEP, simvastatin; Comparator: standard care or alternative intervention arms within each trial.
- Primary endpoints: 28-day survival/mortality.
- Key results: IL-6 mediated the effects of imatinib, anakinra, and low tidal volume ventilation on mortality; higher PEEP and simvastatin did not alter IL-6; higher IL-6 concentrations were associated with increased 28-day mortality (pooled HR for log10-unit increase = 4.83, 95% CI 3.50-6.66).
- Limitations:
- Potential heterogeneity across included trials.
- Observational mediation analysis may not fully establish causality.
- Not all interventions affected IL-6 trajectories.
- Why this matters: Identifying IL-6 as a mediator of therapeutic efficacy supports targeting inflammation in ARDS and COVID-19 to improve survival.
deep_dives.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
deep_dives.title: Interleukin-6 is a mediator of therapeutic efficacy in acute lung injury.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this prospective, randomized physiological study of early septic shock patients, using renal resistive index (RRI) responsiveness to guide higher mean arterial pressure (MAP) targets did not improve renal outcomes among RRI responders, and only exploratory benefits in urine output were seen in nonresponders; thus, RRI-guided MAP titration does not currently support changing clinical practice for renal protection in septic shock.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A decrease in renal resistive index (RRI) during a MAP test does not identify early septic shock patients who benefit from higher MAP targets for renal function improvement, but lack of RRI decrease may indicate those who have increased urine output with higher MAP.

- Study type: Prospective physiologic and randomized study
- Population/setting: Patients in the early phase of septic shock in a medical ICU of a university hospital, without chronic kidney disease or immediate need for renal replacement therapy.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Randomization to low (65-70 mm Hg) versus high (80-85 mm Hg) MAP target for 5 days, stratified by RRI response during a 2-hour MAP test.
- Primary endpoints: Renal outcomes including diuresis, KDIGO stage, need for renal replacement therapy, and serum creatinine.
- Key results: Among 80 randomized patients, 23 (29%) were RRI responders; higher MAP target did not improve renal outcomes in RRI responders, but RRI nonresponders had higher urine output with high MAP target, with no significant differences in other renal parameters.
- Limitations:
- Exploratory findings regarding urine output in RRI nonresponders.
- Single-center study.
- Exclusion of patients with chronic kidney disease or immediate need for renal replacement therapy.
- Why this matters: This study suggests that RRI response to a MAP test is not a reliable bedside tool to guide individualized MAP targets for renal protection in early septic shock, but absence of RRI decrease may help identify patients who could benefit from higher MAP in terms of urine output.
deep_dives.title: Renal Resistive Index Responsiveness to a Mean Arterial Pressure Test As a Guide for Mean Arterial Pressure Target in the Early Phase of Septic Shock: A Physiological Study.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large, multicenter randomized trial (ICECAP), varying the duration of therapeutic hypothermia (6–72 hours) after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest did not identify a single optimal duration for improving 90-day neurological outcomes, suggesting that longer cooling does not provide additional benefit and supporting the use of shorter, clinically practical durations.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Longer durations of therapeutic hypothermia at 33 °C did not improve neurological outcomes in comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

- Study type: Multicenter, randomized, adaptive-allocation clinical trial
- Population/setting: Adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest who remained unconscious, enrolled at 71 US hospitals between June 2020 and June 2025 (N=1158).
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Therapeutic hypothermia at 33 °C for varying durations (6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60, and 72 hours) compared to each other.
- Primary endpoints: Neurological function at 90 days, measured using a weighted modified Rankin Scale score.
- Key results: For nonshockable rhythms, the posterior probability that 6 hours was the shortest duration achieving maximal neurological outcome was 0.51; results were similar for shockable rhythms. No differences in secondary outcomes or mortality were observed across cooling durations.
- Limitations:
- Adaptive randomization may limit direct comparison between all durations.
- Study stopped at interim analysis, possibly affecting power for longer durations.
- Generalizability may be limited to patients meeting strict inclusion criteria.
- Why this matters: These findings suggest that extending the duration of therapeutic hypothermia beyond 6 hours does not provide additional neurological benefit, potentially informing future guidelines and reducing unnecessary resource use.
deep_dives.title: Duration of Therapeutic Hypothermia After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: The ICECAP Randomized Clinical Trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: This protocol describes a large, multicenter randomized controlled trial comparing two backrest positions (5° vs. 35° elevation) in comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, aiming to determine their impact on 90-day mortality; results will provide high-quality evidence to guide positioning practices in post-resuscitation care, where current recommendations are based on limited data.
pubmed.title: Backrest Position and Outcome in Comatose Survivors of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Protocol for a Multi-Center Randomized Comparison Within the Danish Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (DANOHCA) Trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: This large meta-analysis of 45 RCTs (32,215 patients) found no mortality benefit for intensive versus conventional glycemic control in critically ill adults, but intensive targets increased severe hypoglycemia risk and only showed subgroup benefits (e.g., neurologic outcomes in neuro ICU, mortality in cardiac surgery) with evidence limited by study inconsistencies and bias; thus, routine intensive glycemic control is not broadly supported and should be individualized.
pubmed.title: Comparison of Intensive Versus Conventional Glycemic Control Targets: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the 2024 Society of Critical Care Medicine Guidelines on Glycemic Control for Critically Ill Adults.

pubmed.title: The Danish Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Trial: A Statistical Analysis Plan.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this multicenter randomized trial of high-risk hypertensive patients undergoing major abdominal surgery, targeting an intraoperative MAP ≥ 80 mmHg (vs. ≥ 65 mmHg) significantly reduced the incidence of major postoperative organ dysfunction and mortality, as well as acute kidney injury, suggesting that higher MAP targets may improve outcomes in this population.
pubmed.title: HIgh versus STAndard blood Pressure target in hypertensive high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery: the HISTAP multicenter randomized clinical trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: This systematic review found high and variable mortality and severe neurological injury rates following newborn chest compressions at birth, especially among very preterm or very low birth weight infants, but heterogeneity in study definitions and lack of granular data limit the strength and clinical applicability of the evidence, highlighting the need for standardized, prospective research to guide neonatal resuscitation practices.
pubmed.title: A systematic review of mortality and severe morbidities following newborn chest compressions at birth.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this randomized substudy of the BOX trial, targeting a higher mean arterial pressure (77 mmHg vs. 63 mmHg) in comatose out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors led to increased pulmonary artery pressures and right ventricular cardiac power output, with a transient reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance; these findings suggest that higher MAP targets may enhance right ventricular function early after cardiac arrest, though the clinical significance requires further investigation.
pubmed.title: Impact of Higher Versus Lower Blood Pressure Targets on Pulmonary Vascular Hemodynamics During Intensive Care After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this multicenter randomized controlled trial, adding metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) to standard care in sepsis did not significantly improve the primary clinical outcome (DOOR/RADAR score), but secondary outcomes such as duration of mechanical ventilation, shock resolution, and 90-day quality of life were improved without increasing healthcare costs, suggesting potential clinical benefits of mNGS-guided diagnostics despite no primary endpoint effect.
pubmed.title: Effects of a clinical metagenomics intervention on clinical outcomes, healthcare costs, and health-related quality of life in patients with sepsis or septic shock: results of the randomized-controlled DigiSep trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this post hoc analysis of two randomized trials, thiamine supplementation reduced lactate levels only in post-cardiac arrest patients with higher baseline mitochondrial respiration, suggesting that measuring mitochondrial function may help identify those most likely to benefit from thiamine therapy. This highlights the potential for personalized metabolic resuscitation strategies in critically ill patients.
pubmed.title: Baseline measurements of cellular respiration affect the response to thiamine treatment in post-arrest patients.

pubmed.bottom_line: This systematic review and meta-analysis found that supervised aerobic exercise training, especially at high intensity, is associated with greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and reduced postoperative complications compared to unsupervised exercise, although no studies directly compared the two; these findings support prioritizing supervised programs in clinical prehabilitation when feasible.
pubmed.title: Assessing impact of supervision in aerobic exercise training on fitness and clinical outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

pubmed.bottom_line: A simulation-based curriculum integrating CPR coach and compressor training with metronome feedback significantly improved chest compression depth and rate compliance in a pediatric emergency department, especially for infants, while maintaining optimal chest compression fraction; this quality improvement study suggests that structured, multimodal training can enhance adherence to CPR guidelines in real clinical settings.
pubmed.title: Integrated CPR coach and compressor training improves CPR quality in a pediatric emergency department.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this large multicentre randomized trial, using a lower oxygen saturation threshold of 88% (vs 92%) in children with acute respiratory distress safely reduced hospital length of stay without increasing adverse events, suggesting that more permissive oxygen targets may prevent overtreatment and shorten hospitalization.
pubmed.title: Oxygen saturation thresholds in children with acute respiratory distress (OxyKids): a multicentre, open, parallel-group, randomised clinical trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this multicenter randomized controlled trial of adolescents undergoing idiopathic scoliosis correction, intraoperative remifentanil dosing guided by Analgesia Nociception Index monitoring did not reduce postoperative morphine consumption or persistent pain compared to standard hemodynamic guidance, suggesting no clinical benefit for nociception monitoring in this context.
pubmed.title: Effects of Intraoperative Nociception Monitoring during Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis Correction.

pubmed.bottom_line: This prospective observational study found that tactile stimulation in the delivery room is commonly used and associated with a modest heart rate increase in newborns, particularly those with initial HR <140 bpm, but newborns with bradycardia (HR <100 bpm for ≥10 s) in the first minute after birth are four times more likely to require positive pressure ventilation, highlighting the need for close monitoring and readiness to escalate resuscitation in these infants.
pubmed.title: Tactile stimulation and newborn heart rate responses in the delivery room: an observational video study.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this large observational study of high-risk patients, using high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) during breaks from noninvasive ventilation (NIV) after extubation was associated with lower unadjusted extubation failure rates compared to standard oxygen, but this benefit was not statistically significant after adjustment for confounders; further randomized trials are needed to clarify its clinical impact.
pubmed.title: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen during breaks from noninvasive ventilation after extubation: an observational study.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large, multicenter randomized trial of adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared to volatile inhalational anesthesia, indicating no clinically significant difference in recovery or major outcomes between these anesthesia techniques. This evidence suggests that either approach is appropriate for maintenance of anesthesia in this patient population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared with volatile-based inhalational anesthesia in older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Pragmatic, multicenter, open-label randomized clinical trial
- Population/setting: Patients aged 50 years or older scheduled for elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK National Health Service hospitals
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Maintenance of general anesthesia with TIVA (propofol infusion) versus volatile-based inhalational agents
- Primary endpoints: Days alive and at home at 30 days
- Key results: Mean days alive and at home at 30 days were similar between groups (22.5 vs 22.4 days; incidence rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.99-1.02; adjusted P = .68); no significant differences in secondary outcomes except lower rates of thirst, hoarseness, and nausea/vomiting in the TIVA group; two cases of unintentional awareness under anesthesia occurred in the TIVA group.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce bias.
- All other perioperative care was at clinician discretion.
- Study conducted in UK NHS hospitals, which may limit generalizability.
- Why this matters: This study provides high-quality evidence that TIVA does not confer a recovery advantage over inhalational anesthesia for older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, informing anesthetic choice in clinical practice.
deep_dives.title: Total Intravenous vs Volatile Inhalational Anesthesia for Major Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this post hoc analysis of a multicenter RCT involving older adults recovering from septic shock, higher baseline frailty, greater organ dysfunction, and corticosteroid use were independently associated with increased post-ICU frailty at 90 days, highlighting the need for targeted interventions in these high-risk patients; evidence is moderate, based on robust statistical analysis of trial data.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Baseline frailty, organ dysfunction severity, and corticosteroid use independently predict severe postintensive care frailty in older adults recovering from septic shock.

- Study type: Post hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adults aged 65 years or older with septic shock admitted to ICUs in Japan
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Clinical characteristics (including corticosteroid use) and severity scores compared across frailty categories post-ICU
- Primary endpoints: Frailty status at 90 days post-intensive care, classified by the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS)
- Key results: Of 339 survivors at 90 days, 30.4% had no-to-mild frailty, 33.6% moderate, and 36.0% severe frailty; higher presepsis CFS (aOR 2.03 per 1-point increase), higher SOFA scores (aOR 1.16 per 1-point increase), and corticosteroid use (aOR 1.72) were independently associated with worse frailty.
- Limitations:
- Post hoc analysis design
- Limited to older adults in Japanese ICUs
- Potential residual confounding
- Why this matters: Identifying risk factors for post-ICU frailty can inform targeted interventions and management strategies for older septic shock survivors.
deep_dives.title: Postintensive Care Frailty of Older Patients With Septic Shock: A Post Hoc Analysis of a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This large multicenter retrospective study found high adherence to some obstetric anesthesia best practices for cesarean delivery (e.g., timely antibiotics, avoidance of general anesthesia), but substantial gaps remain in areas like perioperative hypothermia prevention and vasopressor infusion use; these findings highlight opportunities for targeted quality improvement, especially in higher-risk patients and off-hours cases.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Adherence to obstetric anesthesia best practice guidelines for cesarean delivery is variable, with the lowest adherence seen for post-spinal vasopressor infusions and the highest for avoidance of general anesthesia.

- Study type: Multicenter retrospective cohort study
- Population/setting: 289,047 cesarean delivery cases in women aged 15-44 from the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group (MPOG) database (2015-2022)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Assessment of adherence to best practice guidelines (timely antibiotics, SBP maintenance, GA avoidance, hypothermia prevention, low-dose neuraxial morphine, vasopressor infusions, ≥25-gauge spinal needles); comparison by patient-, case-, and hospital-level factors
- Primary endpoints: Rates of adherence to best practice guidelines for cesarean delivery and factors associated with adherence
- Key results: Adherence rates: timely antibiotics 86.2%, post-spinal SBP maintenance 96.7%, GA avoidance 97.0%, hypothermia prevention 56.7%, low-dose neuraxial morphine 74.2%, vasopressor infusion 55.4%, ≥25-gauge needle 89.0%; poorer adherence was associated with higher ASA status, off-hours cases, and hospitals lacking obstetric fellowships or 'Center of Excellence' status.
- Limitations:
- Retrospective observational design
- Potential for unmeasured confounding
- Reliance on database accuracy and completeness
- Why this matters: Identifying gaps in adherence to best practices can inform targeted interventions to improve the quality and safety of obstetric anesthesia care for cesarean deliveries.
deep_dives.title: Frequency of adherence to obstetric anesthesia best practices for cesarean delivery: A multicenter retrospective cohort analysis.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 120 cardiac surgery patients, repeated bilateral deep parasternal intercostal plane catheter boluses of ropivacaine did not reduce postoperative pain or opioid consumption compared to placebo, suggesting this intervention does not provide additional analgesic benefit in this setting.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Repeated ropivacaine boluses via bilateral deep parasternal intercostal plane catheters did not improve postoperative pain control or reduce opioid consumption compared to placebo after cardiac surgery.

- Study type: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial
- Population/setting: 120 adult patients undergoing elective coronary artery bypass grafting or heart valve replacement at a single center
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Repeated ropivacaine boluses via bilateral DPIP catheters versus saline placebo for 72 hours postoperatively
- Primary endpoints: Postoperative pain intensity assessed by visual analog scale or behavioral pain scale
- Key results: No significant differences in pain trajectories (P = .77 at rest; P = 1.00 with movement) or cumulative opioid consumption between groups; postoperative nausea and vomiting was more common in the ropivacaine group (46.7% vs 30%), especially among valve surgery patients (60.6% vs 26.5%, P = .012); no differences in sedation or mechanical ventilation times.
- Limitations:
- Single-center study
- Catheter dislodgement and suboptimal positioning occurred
- Dropouts due to pain during injection
- Potential for underpowering to detect small differences
- Why this matters: Routine use of DPIP catheters with repeated ropivacaine boluses after cardiac surgery should be avoided, as it does not improve pain control or reduce opioid use.
deep_dives.title: The Effect of Repeated Bilateral Deep Parasternal Intercostal Plane Catheter Boluses on Analgesia After Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this multicenter, cluster-randomized trial, prehospital initiation of a 1-hour resuscitation bundle for septic shock did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality compared to usual care, suggesting that early aggressive prehospital intervention may not improve short-term survival in this population. This evidence is moderate and clinically relevant for guiding prehospital management protocols in septic shock.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Prehospital initiation of a 1-hour resuscitation bundle did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality in adults with septic shock compared to usual care.

- Study type: Multicenter, open-label, cluster-randomized trial
- Population/setting: Adults with suspected septic shock managed by prehospital mobile ICU teams in France (N=381, mean age 67 ± 15 years)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: 1-hour resuscitation bundle (early antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors, hydrocortisone as needed) versus usual care
- Primary endpoints: 28-day all-cause mortality
- Key results: 28-day mortality was 22% in the 1-hour bundle group and 27% in the usual care group (risk ratio 0.81; 95% CI [0.61-1.08]; p=0.16); secondary outcomes were similar between groups.
- Limitations:
- Imbalances in patient enrollment between centers
- Small difference in care provided between groups
- 17 participants did not consent and were excluded

pubmed.bottom_line: In this large, multicenter randomized trial of adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery, total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared to volatile inhalational anesthesia, indicating no clinically significant difference in recovery or major outcomes between these anesthesia techniques. pubmed.bottom_line: In this secondary analysis of a cluster-randomized controlled trial, an ICU telemedicine program increased the frequency of spontaneous breathing trials and reduced the duration of invasive ventilation among successfully weaned patients, but did not improve overall weaning success rates; these findings suggest telemedicine may enhance certain weaning processes but not ultimate weaning outcomes.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 120 cardiac surgery patients, repeated bilateral deep parasternal intercostal plane catheter boluses of ropivacaine did not reduce postoperative pain or opioid consumption compared to placebo, suggesting this intervention does not provide additional analgesic benefit in this setting.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this multicenter, cluster-randomized trial, prehospital initiation of a 1-hour resuscitation bundle for septic shock did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality compared to usual care, suggesting that early aggressive prehospital intervention may not improve short-term survival in this population. This evidence is moderate and clinically relevant for guiding prehospital management protocols in septic shock.
pubmed.title: A 1-Hour Resuscitation Bundle for Prehospital Management of Septic Shock.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this randomized, double-blind study, the 90% effective dose (ED90) of an initial norepinephrine bolus followed by infusion to prevent postspinal hypotension in elective cesarean delivery was determined, providing evidence to guide optimal dosing and potentially improve maternal and fetal outcomes. This strengthens clinical practice by offering a data-driven approach to norepinephrine prophylaxis in this setting.
pubmed.title: Determination of the 90% Effective Dose of the Initial Bolus of Norepinephrine Followed by a Continuous Infusion to Prevent Hypotension in Elective Cesarean Delivery: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Up-Down Study.

pubmed.bottom_line: This large multicenter observational study found that while renal replacement therapy (RRT) in critically ill ICU patients was associated with increased hospital mortality overall, specific subgroups with severe renal dysfunction (elevated creatinine, low urine output, high BUN) may benefit, highlighting the importance of individualized RRT initiation; evidence is moderate due to observational design but clinically relevant for refining patient selection.
pubmed.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects of Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Observational Study Using a Japanese ICU Registry.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this post hoc analysis of a multicenter RCT involving older adults recovering from septic shock, higher baseline frailty, greater organ dysfunction, and corticosteroid use were independently associated with increased post-ICU frailty at 90 days, highlighting the need for targeted interventions in these high-risk patients; evidence is moderate, based on robust statistical analysis of trial data.
pubmed.title: Postintensive Care Frailty of Older Patients With Septic Shock: A Post Hoc Analysis of a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this phase 3 trial, secukinumab significantly increased sustained remission rates and reduced glucocorticoid exposure in patients with relapsed polymyalgia rheumatica compared to placebo, with a similar safety profile, suggesting it is an effective steroid-sparing option for this population.

pubmed.bottom_line: This historical review highlights that landmark RCTs in intensive care medicine have shifted practice away from intervention intensity and rigid protocols toward individualized, supportive care and harm avoidance, with strong evidence showing that many physiologically appealing interventions do not improve patient-centered outcomes; ongoing questions remain about tailoring therapies to patient heterogeneity, underscoring the need for continued critical appraisal of established and emerging practices.
pubmed.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this single-center randomized trial, elevated cardiopulmonary bypass flow during cardiac surgery significantly reduced early renal injury biomarkers and perioperative norepinephrine requirements without increasing adverse events, though the reduction in clinical AKI incidence was not statistically significant; these findings suggest high-flow CPB may offer renal protection, but larger studies are needed to confirm clinical benefit.
pubmed.title: Elevated Cardiopulmonary Bypass Flow for Renal Protection in Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized Trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: Many randomized trials underpinning perioperative anesthesia guidelines have a low Fragility Index (median 4), indicating that their statistically significant results could be overturned by just a few outcome events; this highlights the need for caution when interpreting guideline recommendations based on such potentially unstable evidence.
pubmed.title: Fragility Index of Randomized Clinical Trials in Perioperative Anesthesia: A Methodological Survey of Guideline-Supporting Evidence.

pubmed.bottom_line: This review highlights a shift in airway management guidelines from focusing solely on anatomical challenges to also addressing physiologically difficult airways, emphasizing the need for clinicians to anticipate and manage both anatomical and physiological risks during airway interventions; this approach is based on expert consensus and aims to improve patient safety in high-risk scenarios.
pubmed.title: From the Anatomically Difficult Airway to the Physiologically Difficult Airway: Lessons From Contemporary Airway Society Guidelines.

pubmed.bottom_line: This pooled analysis of six trials found that colorectal cancer patients with higher baseline physical function and walking distance, especially when combined with low malnutrition risk, had the lowest rates of 30-day postoperative complications after multimodal prehabilitation, suggesting that targeting and optimizing these modifiable factors may improve surgical outcomes.
pubmed.title: Describing Successful Multimodal Prehabilitation Before Colorectal Cancer Resection: A Recursive Partitioning Analysis of Pooled Trial Data.

pubmed.bottom_line: In this randomized, blinded trial of high-risk patients undergoing major non-cardiac surgery, a pre-operative intravenous crystalloid bolus did not significantly reduce post-induction hypotension compared to standard care, suggesting that routine pre-induction crystalloid administration may not be beneficial for preventing hypotension in this population.
pubmed.title: Effect of Pre-operative Intravenous Crystalloid Bolus on Post-Induction Blood Pressure - a randomized blinded intervention trial.

pubmed.bottom_line: This large multicenter retrospective study found high adherence to some obstetric anesthesia best practices for cesarean delivery (e.g., timely antibiotics, avoidance of general anesthesia), but substantial gaps remain in areas like perioperative hypothermia prevention and vasopressor infusion use; these findings highlight opportunities for targeted quality improvement, especially in higher-risk patients and off-hours cases.
pubmed.title: Frequency of adherence to obstetric anesthesia best practices for cesarean delivery: A multicenter retrospective cohort analysis.

pubmed.bottom_line: This systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs found that targeting higher versus lower intraoperative mean arterial pressure (MAP) during noncardiac surgery did not affect 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, or myocardial injury, though only modest MAP differences were achieved between groups; thus, current evidence does not support aggressive intraoperative MAP targets for improving these outcomes.
pubmed.title: Intraoperative hypotension and adverse postoperative outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

pubmed.bottom_line: This large meta-analysis (23 studies, 2,000 patients) shows that diaphragmatic excursion measured by ultrasound is the most reliable parameter for predicting weaning outcomes in mechanically ventilated AECOPD patients, supporting its clinical use to guide weaning decisions in this high-risk group.
pubmed.title: Predictive value of diaphragmatic ultrasound for weaning outcomes in mechanically ventilated patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

pubmed.bottom_line: This large multicenter study validates the Well-Being Influencers Survey for Healthcare (WISH) as a reliable tool for assessing systemic factors influencing occupational well-being in anesthesiology, showing that better well-being culture is strongly associated with lower intention to leave and higher organizational commitment; these findings support using WISH to guide targeted interventions to improve workforce stability and patient care.
pubmed.title: A Multidepartment Investigation of Occupational Well-being, Systemic Features, and Organizational Outcomes in Anesthesiology Using the Well-Being Influencers Survey for Healthcare (WISH).

pubmed.bottom_line: Implementing Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols in Ethiopian hospitals, based on a cluster-randomized trial, was cost-effective—reducing complication-related expenses and hospital stays with minimal additional per-patient costs—suggesting ERAS is a practical and economically beneficial strategy for improving surgical outcomes in low-resource settings.

pubmed.bottom_line: This updated systematic review (176 RCTs, 8 systematic reviews) recommends multimodal analgesia with paracetamol, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, dexamethasone, and single-shot regional blocks (not continuous paravertebral block or gabapentin) for major oncological breast surgery, reflecting strong evidence and guiding clinicians toward safer, more effective pain management strategies.
pubmed.title: Pain management after major oncological breast surgery: an updated systematic review and procedure specific postoperative pain management (PROSPECT) recommendations.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this multicenter phase 3 randomized trial, intravenous arginine did not reduce time to crisis resolution or opioid use in children and adolescents with sickle cell disease acute pain episodes compared to placebo, indicating no clinical benefit and suggesting arginine should not be used for this indication.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Intravenous arginine did not reduce time to crisis resolution compared with placebo in children and young adults with sickle cell disease acute pain episodes.

- Study type: Prospective, phase 3, double-blind randomized clinical trial
- Population/setting: Patients aged 3 to 21 years with sickle cell disease presenting to the emergency department at 10 US children's hospitals for acute pain episodes requiring parenteral opioids.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intravenous arginine (200 mg/kg followed by 100 mg/kg every 8 hours until discharge) versus saline placebo.
- Primary endpoints: Time to crisis resolution, defined as hours from initial study drug delivery to last intravenous opioid dose.
- Key results: Median time to crisis resolution was 60.8 hours for arginine and 65.8 hours for placebo (absolute difference, 7.2 hours; 95% CI, -21.6 to 35.9 hours); no significant differences were found in total parenteral opioid use, pain scores, patient-reported outcomes, or safety events.
- Limitations:
- Trial was halted early for futility.
- Study population limited to children and young adults.
- Conducted only in US children's hospitals.
- Why this matters: There remains a lack of effective FDA-approved therapies for acute pain episodes in sickle cell disease, and intravenous arginine does not provide benefit in this setting.
deep_dives.title: Arginine Therapy for Sickle Cell Disease Acute Pain Episodes: The STArT Randomized Clinical Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this prematurely stopped randomized controlled trial of cancer patients with septic shock and anemia, a liberal red blood cell transfusion strategy (hemoglobin threshold 9.0 g/dL) did not improve lactate clearance or 28-day mortality compared to a restrictive strategy (7.0 g/dL), but was associated with more thrombotic events, suggesting no clinical benefit and potential harm from liberal transfusion in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A liberal red blood cell transfusion strategy did not show superiority over a restrictive strategy in cancer patients with septic shock and was associated with more thrombotic events.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adult patients with hematological or solid malignancies and septic shock (lactate >2.0 mmol/L, hemoglobin <9.0 g/dL) in 18 centers in France
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Liberal RBC transfusion (hemoglobin threshold 9.0 g/dL) versus restrictive RBC transfusion (hemoglobin threshold 7.0 g/dL) during first 48 hours of resuscitation
- Primary endpoints: 12-hour lactate reduction (normalization ≤2.0 mmol/L or relative decrease by 30% from baseline)
- Key results: 12-hour lactate reduction was achieved in 52% (liberal) vs. 50% (restrictive) (OR 1.07; 95% CI 0.60–1.90; P=0.82); thrombotic events were higher in the liberal group (13% vs. 1%; P=0.001); 28-day mortality was 46% (liberal) vs. 53% (restrictive) (P=0.34).
- Limitations:
- Trial was stopped early for safety concerns.
- Did not reach planned sample size.
- Potential imbalance in adverse events.
- Why this matters: This study informs transfusion strategies in cancer patients with septic shock, suggesting no benefit to a liberal approach and highlighting increased thrombotic risk.
deep_dives.title: Early red blood cell transfusion strategy in septic shock among patients with cancer: the TRANSPORT randomized controlled trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this single-center randomized controlled trial, a mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg was non-inferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index alarm in preventing intraoperative hypotension during elective non-cardiac surgery, suggesting that simpler MAP alarms may be as effective as more complex predictive indices for blood pressure management in this setting.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: A mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg is non-inferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index (>85) alarm for preventing intraoperative hypotension in elective non-cardiac surgery.

- Study type: Blinded, single-center, randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adults undergoing moderate- or high-risk elective non-cardiac surgery with continuous arterial pressure monitoring at a single center (N=143)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mean arterial pressure alarm (<72 mmHg) versus Hypotension Prediction Index alarm (>85)
- Primary endpoints: Area under the threshold for mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg
- Key results: Median area under the hypotension threshold was 3.75 [0.00-22.62] mmHg⋅min (MAP group) vs 4.00 [0.00-19.00] mmHg⋅min (HPI group); mean difference after log-transformation was 0.03 (95% CI: -0.24 to 0.29), meeting non-inferiority criteria. No significant differences were found in secondary hemodynamic metrics, alarm characteristics, patient outcomes, or medication/fluid administration.
- Limitations:
- Single-center study
- Sample size may limit detection of rare adverse events
- Blinding details not fully described
- Why this matters: A simple and widely available MAP alarm set at 72 mmHg can effectively prevent intraoperative hypotension, offering a pragmatic and cost-effective alternative to proprietary prediction algorithms.
deep_dives.title: Hypotension Prediction Index versus Mean Arterial Pressure Alarm for Preventing Intraoperative Hypotension in Elective Non-Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this randomized controlled trial, adding multiplex PCR (FilmArray Pneumonia Panel) to conventional microbiology did not significantly increase targeted antibiotic therapy at 24 hours in all patients with suspected ventilator-associated or hospital-acquired pneumonia, but did show benefit in those with culture-confirmed pneumonia; this suggests PCR may be most useful for guiding therapy when infection is microbiologically documented.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Adding the FilmArray Pneumonia Panel (FAPP) to conventional microbiology did not significantly increase targeted antibiotic therapy at 24 hours in all patients with suspected VAP or vHAP, but showed benefit in those with culture-confirmed pneumonia.

- Study type: Open-label, multicenter randomized-controlled trial
- Population/setting: Immunocompetent adults with suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia or hospital-acquired pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation in intensive care units; 146 patients analyzed across multiple centers.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: FAPP plus conventional microbiology versus conventional microbiology alone.
- Primary endpoints: Proportion of patients receiving targeted antimicrobial therapy 24 hours after inclusion.
- Key results: Targeted therapy at 24 hours was achieved in 35.1% of the FAPP group vs 23.6% of controls (absolute difference 11.5%, 95% CI -0.03 to 26.2, p=0.13); in culture-confirmed pneumonia, rates were 55.3% vs 31.0% (absolute difference 24.2%, 95% CI 1.1 to 47.4, p=0.048). Secondary outcomes did not differ significantly.
- Limitations:
- Single-blind design may introduce bias.
- Sample size may be insufficient to detect smaller differences.
- Only immunocompetent adults were included, limiting generalizability.
- 10 patients excluded post-randomization due to lack of consent.
- Why this matters: Rapid molecular diagnostics like FAPP may improve targeted antibiotic use in confirmed pneumonia cases, but routine use in all suspected cases may not provide significant benefit.
deep_dives.title: Impact of a strategy using multiplex PCR on targeted antibiotic therapy for patients with suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia or hospital-acquired pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation: a randomized, single-blind trial.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This matching-adjusted indirect comparison found no significant difference between mepolizumab and dupilumab in reducing exacerbations or improving quality of life in patients with COPD and an eosinophilic phenotype, suggesting either agent may be similarly effective for this population, though direct head-to-head trials are lacking.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Mepolizumab and dupilumab showed no statistically significant difference in reducing exacerbations or improving health-related quality of life in COPD patients with an eosinophilic phenotype.

- Study type: Matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) using pooled data from Phase III randomized, placebo-controlled trials.
- Population/setting: Patients with COPD and an eosinophilic phenotype (blood eosinophil counts ≥300 cells/μL, mMRC ≥2, moderate-to-severe airflow limitation, and chronic bronchitis) from Phase III clinical trials.
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mepolizumab versus dupilumab as add-on maintenance treatments.
- Primary endpoints: Annualized rate of moderate/severe exacerbations and changes in health-related quality of life (SGRQ-C).
- Key results: No statistically significant differences in annualized exacerbation rates (rate ratio [95% CI]: 0.91 [0.60, 1.37] with investigator-assessed CB; 1.13 [0.80, 1.58] with SGRQ-C CB definition) or SGRQ-C changes between mepolizumab and dupilumab.
- Limitations:
- Indirect comparison rather than head-to-head randomized trial.
- Potential residual confounding despite propensity score matching.
- Differences in trial eligibility criteria and definitions of chronic bronchitis.
- Why this matters: This study informs clinicians that mepolizumab and dupilumab have similar efficacy for reducing exacerbations and improving quality of life in COPD patients with an eosinophilic phenotype, aiding treatment selection.
deep_dives.title: Mepolizumab and Dupilumab Show No Significant Difference in Reducing Exacerbations in Patients with COPD and an Eosinophilic Phenotype: Matching-Adjusted Indirect Treatment Comparison.

BOTTOM LINE: A mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg is non-inferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index (>85) alarm for preventing intraoperative hypotension in elective non-cardiac surgery.

- Study type: Blinded, single-center, randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adults undergoing moderate- or high-risk elective non-cardiac surgery with continuous arterial pressure monitoring at a single center (N=143)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Mean arterial pressure alarm (<72 mmHg) versus Hypotension Prediction Index alarm (>85)
- Primary endpoints: Area under the threshold for mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg
- Key results: Median area under the hypotension threshold was 3.75 [0.00-22.62] mmHg⋅min (MAP group) vs 4.00 [0.00-19.00] mmHg⋅min (HPI group); mean difference after log-transformation was 0.03 (95% CI: -0.24 to 0.29), meeting non-inferiority criteria. - Limitations:
- Single-center study
- Sample size may limit detection of rare adverse events
- Blinding details not fully described
- Why this matters: A simple and widely available MAP alarm set at 72 mmHg can effectively prevent intraoperative hypotension, offering a pragmatic and cost-effective alternative to proprietary prediction algorithms.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large randomized controlled trial, physiotherapist-led care for uncomplicated musculoskeletal conditions in the emergency department was found to be effective, safe, and cost-effective compared to usual physician- or nurse practitioner-led care, suggesting that physiotherapists can play a key role in improving emergency department efficiency and patient outcomes for these conditions.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Physiotherapist-led care in the emergency department for uncomplicated musculoskeletal conditions reduces length of stay, is safe, and is cost-effective compared to usual care.

- Study type: Open-label, pragmatic, randomized controlled trial with economic evaluation
- Population/setting: Adults aged 18 years and older with uncomplicated musculoskeletal conditions presenting to five emergency departments in New South Wales, Australia
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Physiotherapist-led care versus usual physician-led or nurse practitioner-led care
- Primary endpoints: Length of stay in the emergency department (time from arrival to discharge)
- Key results: Mean length of stay was 2.4 hours in the intervention group versus 3.4 hours in the control group (difference -1.0 h, 95% CI -1.2 to -0.8); adverse events were similar between groups (6.6% vs 5.9%, p=0.72); intervention group had lower costs (-$35.1, 95% CI -69.0 to -1.7) and a 98.1% probability of being cost-effective.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce performance bias
- Conducted only in New South Wales, Australia, which may limit generalizability
- Why this matters: Implementing physiotherapist-led care in emergency departments can improve efficiency and reduce costs without compromising patient safety for musculoskeletal presentations.
deep_dives.title: Physiotherapist-led care for musculoskeletal conditions in the emergency department (RESHAP-ED): a randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large prospective cohort study, adding CT-based body composition metrics (skeletal muscle area, muscle radiodensity, and subcutaneous fat radiodensity) to standard risk models improved prediction of 30-day postoperative cardiovascular events in patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery, suggesting these imaging biomarkers may enhance preoperative risk stratification.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: CT-derived body composition metrics enhance the prediction of postoperative cardiovascular events beyond conventional clinical predictors in patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

- Study type: Prospective cohort study
- Population/setting: Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors undergoing major noncardiac surgery in the multicenter PREVENGE-CB cohort and its Nanfang extension (N=1,594).
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Addition of CT-based body composition metrics (skeletal muscle area, muscle radiodensity, subcutaneous fat radiodensity) to standard clinical risk models versus standard clinical risk models alone.
- Primary endpoints: Composite cardiovascular events within 30 days after surgery.
- Key results: The addition of three CT-based body composition metrics improved discrimination for postoperative cardiovascular events over the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (ΔAUC = 0.136; 95% CI, 0.083 to 0.188), Gupta risk calculator (ΔAUC = 0.032; 95% CI, -0.002 to 0.065), and a refitted clinical model (ΔAUC = 0.035; 95% CI, 0.008 to 0.062); findings were validated in an independent cohort.
- Limitations:
- Potential generalizability limitations due to study population.
- CT imaging may not be routinely available for all surgical candidates.
- The study does not address cost-effectiveness or implementation feasibility.
- Why this matters: Incorporating CT-based body composition analysis into preoperative assessment may improve cardiovascular risk stratification and guide perioperative management.
deep_dives.title: Computed Tomography-based Body Composition Assessment for Preoperative Cardiovascular Risk Prediction: A Prospective Cohort Study.

deep_dives.bottom_line: In this large, post hoc analysis of two clinical trials, intraoperative corticosteroids at antiemetic doses did not significantly reduce postoperative pulmonary complications in major surgery patients, though a modest improvement in oxygenation was observed; these findings suggest routine corticosteroid use for pulmonary protection is not supported.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Intraoperative corticosteroid administration at antiemetic doses did not reduce postoperative pulmonary complications in adults undergoing major abdominal or thoracic surgery, though it modestly improved postoperative pulmonary gas exchange.

- Study type: Post hoc analysis of two clinical trials
- Population/setting: Adult patients undergoing major abdominal or thoracic surgeries across 30 hospitals (N=1963)
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Intraoperative corticosteroid administration at antiemetic doses versus no corticosteroid administration
- Primary endpoints: Composite of postoperative pulmonary complications within 30 days after surgery
- Key results: After weighting for confounders, corticosteroids were not associated with a significant reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.62-1.18, P=0.347); however, there was a modest improvement in arterial oxygenation (adjusted mean difference 19.9 mm Hg, 95% CI 0.64-39.1, P=0.043).
- Limitations:
- Post hoc analysis design
- Potential residual confounding despite weighting
- Findings may not generalize beyond major abdominal or thoracic surgeries
- Why this matters: This study informs perioperative management by showing that routine intraoperative corticosteroids at antiemetic doses do not reduce pulmonary complications, supporting their safety but not efficacy for this outcome.
deep_dives.title: Intraoperative corticosteroid administration and postoperative pulmonary complications: a secondary analysis of the iPROVE clinical trials.

BOTTOM LINE: A structured early mobilization program for mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis or acute respiratory failure did not improve functional status at ICU discharge or at 12 months compared to usual care.

- Study type: Multicenter randomized open-label controlled trial
- Population/setting: Adult patients with sepsis or respiratory failure requiring invasive ventilation for ≥48 hours in five tertiary hospitals in South Korea
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Structured six-step early mobilization program versus usual care
- Primary endpoints: Functional Status Score for the ICU (FSS-ICU) at ICU discharge
- Key results: No significant difference in FSS-ICU at ICU discharge between groups (mean 23.6 vs. 22.2; P = 0.44); intervention group mobilized earlier and more often; long-term outcomes improved similarly in both groups over 12 months.
- Limitations:
- Open-label design may introduce bias
- Study conducted only in South Korea, limiting generalizability
- Sample size may limit detection of small differences
- Why this matters: This study challenges the assumption that protocolized early mobilization improves short- or long-term functional outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients, informing ICU rehabilitation practices.

deep_dives.bottom_line: This randomized controlled trial found that moderate to deep neuromuscular blockade significantly reduces both the incidence and severity of the oculocardiac reflex during pediatric strabismus surgery compared to minimal to shallow blockade, suggesting that deeper blockade may improve intraoperative cardiac safety in this population.
deep_dives.deep_dive_markdown:
BOTTOM LINE: Moderate to deep neuromuscular blockade significantly reduces the incidence and severity of the oculocardiac reflex during pediatric strabismus surgery compared to minimal to shallow blockade.

- Study type: Prospective, double-blinded randomized controlled trial
- Population/setting: 204 pediatric patients aged 3 to 18 years undergoing strabismus surgery under general anesthesia
- Intervention/exposure & comparator: Moderate to deep neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four count 0 to 3) versus minimal to shallow neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four count of 4 with ratio less than 0.9)
- Primary endpoints: Incidence of oculocardiac reflex grade greater than or equal to 2 (heart rate decrease ≥20% from baseline)
- Key results: OCR grade ≥2 occurred less in the moderate to deep group (30.3%) than the minimal to shallow group (53.9%; OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.66, P=0.001); severe OCR (grade ≥3) was also reduced (18.2% vs 35.3%; OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21–0.78, P=0.007); magnitude and duration of heart rate reduction were both smaller in the moderate to deep group.
- Limitations:
- Single surgical procedure and pediatric population may limit generalizability.
- No long-term outcomes reported.
- Why this matters: Optimizing neuromuscular blockade depth can reduce the risk and severity of oculocardiac reflex, improving safety during pediatric strabismus surgery.
deep_dives.title: Neuromuscular Blockade Depth and Oculocardiac Reflex in Pediatric Strabismus Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
